title: A central maximal torus forces nilpotence
statement: Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure]. All groups are affine group schemes [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism] over $k$, and all subgroups are closed subgroup schemes [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. Smoothness and connectedness have the meanings of [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-connected-scheme]. A torus is a group scheme isomorphic to $(\mathbf G_m)^r$ for an integer $r\geq0$ [def-sc-gm-ga]; a maximal torus is one not properly contained in another torus subgroup. A group is solvable if its successive scheme-theoretic commutator subgroups eventually become trivial. Let $H$ be smooth and connected, and let $S\subseteq H$ be a maximal torus which is central: for every commutative $k$-algebra $A$, every $s\in S(A)$ and $h\in H(A)$ commute. Then $H$ is nilpotent, meaning that there is a finite descending series of closed subgroup schemes $H=H_0\supseteq H_1\supseteq\cdots\supseteq H_m=1$ with $[H,H_i]\subseteq H_{i+1}$, where brackets denote the closed subgroup scheme generated by commutators after scalar extension. In particular $H$ is solvable.

source.place: Proposition 17.23, implication (d) to (a) to (b) to (c), printed p.359, as used in Proposition 17.28, printed p.360; nilpotent groups are solvable by their central series.

proof.text: The identity gives a $k$-point of $H$, so [lem-sbc-connected-rational-point-geometrically-connected] makes $H$ geometrically connected. Centrality makes $S$ normal on every test algebra. Apply [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry] to obtain the faithfully flat finitely presented quotient $q:H\to Q=H/S$, with kernel $S$. Its statement gives that $Q$ is affine of finite type, smooth and geometrically connected, hence connected.

source.place: Theorem 5.28, Proposition 1.62(b), and Proposition 5.59; quotient setup for Proposition 16.60. Connectedness under extension is Stacks Tag 04KV, varieties.tex, lemma-geometrically-connected-if-connected-and-point.

proof.text: By [lem-sfb-quotient-borel-torus-images], the scheme-theoretic image $q(S)$ is a maximal torus of $Q$: its hypotheses hold because $q$ is faithfully flat and $H,Q$ are smooth and connected. Since $S=\ker(q)$, that image is the trivial subgroup. Every torus contains this trivial subgroup, so maximality of $q(S)=1$ says directly that $Q$ has no nontrivial torus.

source.place: Proposition 17.20, printed pp.357--358, maximal-torus image clause.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-no-torus-unipotent] to $Q$ over the algebraically closed field $k$. It supplies a closed faithful matrix representation whose $k$-points are unipotent. These are exactly the geometric points needed in [lem-sfb-geometric-unipotence-unitriangular-embedding], since $k$ is its own algebraic closure. That node yields a closed immersion $i:Q\hookrightarrow\mathcal U_n$ for some $n\geq1$, where $\mathcal U_n$ is the upper unitriangular group scheme.

source.place: Proposition 16.60, printed p.346; Corollary 14.12 and Theorem 14.5, printed pp.281--283.

proof.text: For a commutative $k$-algebra $A$, let $J_r(A)$ be the strictly upper triangular matrices whose entries vanish when $j-i<r$. Put $J_t=0$ for $t\geq n$. Matrix multiplication gives $J_aJ_b\subseteq J_{a+b}$: each nonzero summand uses an intermediate index with distances at least $a$ and $b$. Each $J_r$ is a two-sided ideal in the ring of upper triangular matrices. Thus $F_r(A)=I+J_r(A)$ is a subgroup, using $(I+X)^{-1}=I-X+\cdots+(-X)^{n-1}$; these functors are closed subgroup schemes, cut out by the entries of distance less than $r$, by [def-weil-closed-immersion, def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. For $X\in J_1(A)$ and $Y\in J_r(A)$ one has $[I+X,I+Y]-I=(XY-YX)(I+X)^{-1}(I+Y)^{-1}\in J_{r+1}(A)$. Consequently $[\mathcal U_n,F_r]\subseteq F_{r+1}$, $F_1=\mathcal U_n$ and $F_n=1$. All formulas hold over every $A$, including nonreduced algebras, so they give subgroup-scheme containments rather than just containments on $k$-points.

source.place: Example 6.49, printed pp.136--137, superdiagonal series; Proposition 14.21, printed pp.284--285. Explicit grouped matrix calculation.

proof.text: Define $P_r\subseteq H$ by the equations that the entries of $i(q(h))-I$ of distance less than $r$ vanish, for $1\leq r\leq n$. Pulling back the coordinate equations makes these closed subschemes by [def-weil-closed-immersion]; they are subgroup schemes by [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup], since $i\circ q$ is a homomorphism and each $F_r(A)$ is a subgroup. They descend from $P_1=H$ to $P_n=\ker(i\circ q)=S$, since $i$ is a closed immersion and hence injective on all test algebras. For every $A$, $h\in H(A)$ and $x\in P_r(A)$, step 4 shows $[h,x]\in P_{r+1}(A)$. Appending $P_{n+1}=1$ gives the final inclusion $[H,P_n]=[H,S]=1$ by the assumed centrality of $S$. Reindexing $H_j=P_{j+1}$ for $0\leq j\leq n$ is the required finite central series. Because the containments hold on every algebra and after every scalar extension, the closed subgroups generated by these commutators are contained as well.

source.place: Proposition 14.21, intersection construction; central-kernel pullback of that construction, yielding the conclusion of Proposition 17.23, printed p.359.

proof.text: Let $D^0H=H$ and let $D^{j+1}H$ be the closed subgroup scheme generated by commutators of $D^jH$ after scalar extension. Inductively $D^jH\subseteq H_j$: the base case is equality, and $[D^jH,D^jH]\subseteq[H,H_j]\subseteq H_{j+1}$ proves the step, since $H_{j+1}$ is closed. Thus $D^nH=1$, proving solvability in the precise sense of the statement. When $n=1$, the construction simply reads $H=S\supseteq1$ and uses centrality; it also covers the trivial group and rank-zero $S$.

source.place: Proposition 14.21, nilpotent implies solvable; elementary comparison of derived series with the constructed central series.

proof_origin.place: Quotient and unitriangular proof assembled from Proposition 17.20, Proposition 16.60, Theorem 14.5 and the explicit superdiagonal argument in 6.49/14.21. It proves Proposition 17.23 directly without repeating its Borel dimension induction.

lean.statement: theorem central_maximal_torus_nilpotent (k : Type u) [Field k] [IsAlgClosed k] (H S : Grp (Over (Spec (.of k)))) (iS : S ⟶ H) (haff : IsAffine H.X.left) (hft : LocallyOfFiniteType H.X.hom) (hqc : QuasiCompact H.X.hom) (hsm : Smooth H.X.hom) (hconn : ConnectedSpace H.X.left) (hmax : ReductiveTorusCentralizer.IsMaximalTorus iS) (hcentral : ∀ (A : Type u) [CommRing A] [Algebra k A] (s : StandardGroupSchemes.affine k A ⟶ S.X) (h : StandardGroupSchemes.affine k A ⟶ H.X), Commute (s ≫ iS.hom.hom) h) : (∃ (m : ℕ) (C : Fin (m + 1) → Grp (Over (Spec (.of k)))) (i : ∀ j : Fin (m + 1), C j ⟶ H), (∀ j : Fin (m + 1), IsClosedSubgroupScheme (i j).hom.hom) ∧ IsIso (i 0) ∧ Nonempty (C (Fin.last m) ≅ Grp.trivial _) ∧ (∀ j : Fin m, ∃ l : C j.succ ⟶ C j.castSucc, l ≫ i j.castSucc = i j.succ) ∧ ∀ (j : Fin m) (A : Type u) [CommRing A] [Algebra k A] (h : StandardGroupSchemes.affine k A ⟶ H.X) (c : StandardGroupSchemes.affine k A ⟶ (C j.castSucc).X), ∃ z : StandardGroupSchemes.affine k A ⟶ (C j.succ).X, z ≫ (i j.succ).hom.hom = h * (c ≫ (i j.castSucc).hom.hom) * h⁻¹ * (c ≫ (i j.castSucc).hom.hom)⁻¹) ∧ IsSolvableGroupScheme H.X
